source: Corrêa, Pereira, Seipp (2025) Classical Planning with LLM-Generated Heuristics (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: The LLM writes many domain-specific heuristic functions as Python code. Each is scored on training tasks with greedy best-first search. The best one is kept. The search stays sound, so every plan is correct.
numbers: 8 domains listed, 720 test tasks in the sum row. Pyperplan GBFS coverage: hFF 234, DeepSeek R1 heuristic 373, DeepSeek V3 343, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking 305. End-to-end LLM planning: R1 174, Gemini Thinking 202, Gemini Flash 19. n=25 heuristics per domain. API cost for all V3 and R1 heuristics: $0.25 and $6.12.
limits: Test tasks are larger than training tasks but the domains are known IPC ones. Comparison is in slow Python; C++ hFF is faster per node.
agent_relevance: A model is better used to write a scoring function that code checks than to give the answer. Fits the schema rule that code selects and the model fills slots.

source: Corrêa et al. (2025) prompt ablation (Table 4 of the same paper)
finding: Removing prompt parts hurts. Replacing domain-dependent example heuristics with domain-independent ones (goal count plus four delete-relaxation heuristics from Pyperplan) still worked. With no example heuristic at all, every generated heuristic scored coverage 0. Variance across samples is huge, so selection on training tasks leaves gains unused.
numbers: Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, 25 heuristics per variant, 5-minute limit. Best coverage: original prompt 423 vs 359 to 404 in ablations. Original prompt: worst 114, average 267.0, SD 94.3, 64 failed heuristics out of 200. Training-set selection got 38.7% less than the best-of-pool oracle.
quote: completely removing the example heuristics yields a coverage of 0 for all generated heuristics
limits: Best-case numbers are an oracle over the test set, not a usable method.
agent_relevance: Delete-relaxation heuristics are a useful seed example in the prompt. A selector on held-out checks loses a lot to the oracle, so G3 and G5 apply and a better selector is worth building.

source: Corrêa et al. (2025) memorisation and obfuscation tests
finding: Gains are not only recalled heuristics. In a changed Spanner domain (spanners no longer break) the best generated heuristic gave optimal plan lengths. Renaming all symbols in Blocksworld cut the LLM heuristic but not hFF.
numbers: Blocksworld R1 heuristic solved 66 tasks vs 40 in the obfuscated version; hFF 27 vs 28. New unreleased domain Rod-Rings with o3: 58 tasks vs hFF 59 in Fast Downward.
limits: One model per test; few domains.
agent_relevance: LLM-made relaxed reasoning leans on name semantics. Obfuscated or novel framings are the right stress test for any relaxation operator.

source: Tuisov, Vernik, Shleyfman (2026) Successor-Generator Planning with LLM-generated Heuristics
finding: The LLM writes a problem-specific heuristic in Rust from a successor generator, goal test and initial state (no PDDL needed). Running 10 generated heuristics, each for a slice of the time (SelfPortfolio-10), gave the best result. Non-reasoning GPT-4.1 won once generation time and cost counted.
numbers: 400-task suite. GPT-4.1 with SP-10 solved 276. A post-hoc portfolio of the best classic heuristic plus the LLM reached 304 (authors call it unfair). Six models tested (GPT-4.1, 4.1-mini, GPT-5.1, 5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5). Higher reasoning effort in GPT-5.1 improved heuristics a little and halved compile errors, but fewer fitted in the time budget.
limits: Leaving PDDL sometimes hurt (a reimplemented hmd did worse than ENHSP in Hydropower and Plant Watering). Models struggle with opaque variable names (Pathways, Settlers).
agent_relevance: Diverse sampled heuristics under a time split beat one careful heuristic. Fits G4 (samples are cheap, agreement is not proof) and anytime allocation across candidates.

source: Tuisov et al. (2026) instance-specific vs domain-level heuristics
finding: Showing the model the specific instance (IS) did not help non-reasoning GPT-4.1 in most domains. It helped in FO-Counters and Twin Prime. The best setting was domain-level heuristics from a non-reasoning model run as SP-10.
numbers: Table 2 totals over 400 tasks, domain-dependent: 234 (first compilation), 272 (SP-10) vs IS 195/255/259 in the other columns. Column mapping partly unclear in the extracted text, so read the pattern only: IS did not beat DD overall.
limits: Some table cells could not be read cleanly from the PDF text.
agent_relevance: Per-instance relaxation by the model is not clearly better than one reusable domain heuristic.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas, Sohrabi (2024) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through the Lens of Efficiency
finding: Instead of calling the LLM at every search node, the LLM writes the successor function and goal test once, as code, then a normal search runs. This keeps soundness and completeness and needs few LLM calls.
numbers: 100% accuracy on four search problems. 24 Game: all 1362 tasks solved by a correct successor function and goal test, found after 2.8 and 1 iterations on average in one set. The compared Tree of Thoughts style methods need hundreds of LLM calls per task.
quote: we can solve the entire datasets with 100% accuracy with only a few calls to the LLM
limits: Needs tests or a human to catch code errors. No heuristic guidance in the main results (left for future work).
agent_relevance: Pushing the model's work into generated checkers and letting code search is supported. A relaxed-problem solver is the natural next piece.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: The model scores partial states as sure / maybe / impossible by short lookahead. This is a prompt-based heuristic with pruning. It is not a relaxation: it asks the model to judge, with no solver.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%.
limits: The evaluator is a model judgement and can be wrong; the paper reports cases where all candidate thoughts are invalid.
agent_relevance: A judged lookahead gave large gains where pruning is easy. The schema prefers counted checks over judged ones (G5), so a relaxed solver would replace the judge.

source: Silver et al. (2024) Generalized Planning in PDDL Domains with Pretrained Large Language Models
finding: GPT-4 writes a Python program (told not to use search) that plans for a whole domain. Automatic debugging with checker feedback is the biggest lever. A written strategy summary (CoT) helps unevenly. This solves a general, simpler policy problem instead of each instance.
numbers: 7 domains, 10 seeds, 30 evaluation tasks per seed. GPT-4: Forest 1.00, Delivery 0.90, Gripper 0.90, Ferry 0.80, Heavy 0.60, Spanner 0.10, Miconic 0.01. No debugging: Delivery 0.10, Gripper 0.50, Forest 0.62. No CoT: Ferry 0.20 (CoT helps), Heavy 1.00 (CoT hurts). GPT-3.5 mostly 0.00 (Forest 0.32).
limits: Run through a chat interface; averaged over conversations; only two training tasks fit in the prompt.
agent_relevance: Checker feedback on the model's own program is the main gain. Matches G2 (revise from real failing output). Strategy summaries are not safe to add by default (G1).

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) PlanBench, appendix A.4.2 on model relaxations
finding: The authors graded GPT-4 plans against delete-relaxed, precondition-relaxed and both-relaxed domain models, to see if plans were nearly right. Even in the most lenient grading many plans still failed.
numbers: Blocksworld plan generation: GPT-4 34.3%, InstructGPT-3 6.8%. Mystery (obfuscated) Blocksworld plan generation: GPT-4 26/600 (4.3%) in one setting and 12/600 (2%) in another; InstructGPT-3 14/600 and 6/600.
limits: The relaxed-grading percentages are in a figure that was not readable as text.
agent_relevance: Lenient relaxed checking shows the plans are wrong in structure, not just in small details. A relaxed check cannot rescue them.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2023) On the Planning Abilities of Large Language Models: A Critical Investigation
finding: A search snippet reports that GPT-4 Blocksworld plans checked under delete plus precondition relaxed models are still about 39% incorrect.
numbers: About 39% still incorrect under the most relaxed check, Blocksworld (search snippet, not verified).
limits: The PDF download was corrupt and could not be opened.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as PlanBench: lenient relaxed checking does not fix LLM plans.

source: Stein, Fiser, Hoffmann, Koller (2025) Automating the Generation of Prompts for LLM-based Action Choice in PDDL Planning
finding: On 13 PDDL domains, GPT-4o picks actions step by step from natural-language prompts made from PDDL. ReAct-style thinking gave the best LLM result. It stays well below symbolic planners that use relaxation heuristics.
numbers: 260 tasks (20 per domain). Best LLM (ReAct, PDDL2NL) 194; random 13; breadth-first search 258; A* with LM-cut 240; GBFS with hFF 260. Authors also say that in some domains the best LLM setting scales further than A* with LM-cut.
limits: Small instances (optimal plan length 3 to 20), 5 seeds for LLM runs; cost limited the size.
agent_relevance: A cheap relaxation heuristic (hFF) beats a strong LLM used as planner. LLM-as-planner is the weak baseline; LLM-as-heuristic-writer is the strong one.

source: Hirsch, Uziel, Anaby-Tavor (2024) What's the Plan? Evaluating and Developing Planning-Aware Techniques for Language Models (SimPlan)
finding: LLMs are poor world models and poor at ordering goals. A fine-tuned LM used as the heuristic inside GBFS, with an external state updater, solves classic domains. Without the state update, performance collapsed.
numbers: Describing the next state: GPT-4 average 69%, Llama-3 39%; success falls on average 80% from 1 action to 7. Goal ordering used LAMA landmark orderings as test items (50% is chance): scores around .52 to .69, in 2 of 4 domains not clearly above chance. SimPlan simple/complex: Blocks 1.0/.56, Ferry 1.0/1.0, Grippers 1.0/1.0, Depots 1.0/.12, Minigrid 1.0/.86. Ablation average: full .81, no state update .21, no data augmentation .19.
limits: SimPlan is fine-tuned per domain; a goal-count baseline did well in some domains (Ferry complex 1.0).
agent_relevance: Landmark orderings are where models do poorly, so any model-proposed ordering needs checking. Keep state tracking in code, not in the model.

source: Bukkapatnam, Karuturi (2026) LM-Landmarks (ICML 2026 listing)
finding: The LLM proposes landmark facts from the task text. Each is checked by a delete-relaxation test on the PDDL before use. Only verified landmarks join the landmark-count heuristic, so hallucinations cannot break soundness.
numbers: 8 IPC domains with Fast Downward: coverage +7.5 points over FF and +3.1 over LAMA; search nodes down 41% and 37%; no loss of plan optimality. Authors prove admissibility stays and node savings depend on the LM's landmark recall.
limits: Only the abstract page was read; no arXiv version found; single source, not reproduced.
agent_relevance: The cleanest 'model proposes, relaxation verifies' example. Template for an operator: propose a must-pass subgoal, test it with a cheap relaxed check.

source: Canonaco, Pozanco, Borrajo (2026) Semantic Partial Grounding via LLMs
finding: The LLM drops objects and action schemas it judges irrelevant before grounding. The simplified task is faster to search but can lose solvability, so this is a relaxation that is not sound.
numbers: 175 tasks: full grounding gave valid plans for 161; LLM grounding 139; PLOI 90 of 100. 36 of 175 reformulated tasks could not give valid plans for the original task. Up to two orders of magnitude fewer operators. LAMA solved 10 tasks that full grounding could not. Examples dropped: zoom in Zenotravel, move-b-to-b in Blocksworld.
limits: Loses completeness; a fallback to full grounding is needed.
agent_relevance: Dropping parts of a problem helps but is unsafe. Every simplified version needs a fallback to the original, and a pass on the simplified version is not a pass on the real one.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Learn to Relax with LLMs: AutoCO (ACL 2026)
finding: The LLM proposes how far to relax each constraint; MCTS explores relaxation trajectories and evolution polishes solutions. Relaxed feasible regions made search easier than the original constraints and than expert-set relaxation.
numbers: SFL-8: original constraints plateau at 52% success; AutoCO strategy rises to 80%, 1.1 times the expert strategy at 2500 iterations. SFL-5 (Dual): AutoCO 53%. VRPTW-fuel optimality gap: AutoCO 0.31 (S) and 0.00 (M) vs ReEvo 0.36 and 0.20; FunSearch 1.30 (S).
limits: Operations-research constraint problems, not text reasoning. Author-reported only.
agent_relevance: A model can choose which constraint to loosen and by how much, with search and a checker outside it. Supports an O4 'drop a constraint' operator where code controls the amount.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in LLMs
finding: Ask a higher-level question first (what principle applies?), then answer with it. This is abstraction, close to relaxation, but it does not solve a simpler problem. Gains are large on knowledge tasks and small for a strong model with CoT.
numbers: PaLM-2L: MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2, Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8; TimeQA 41.5 to 66.0 (68.7 with RAG); MuSiQue 35.5 to 42.6; StrategyQA 82.8 to 82.7. GPT-4 + CoT vs Step-Back: Physics 82.9 vs 84.5, Chemistry 85.3 vs 85.6. On Physics it fixes 20.5% of baseline errors and adds 11.9% new ones. Averages over 5 runs.
limits: Most remaining errors were reasoning errors, not abstraction errors. No gain on StrategyQA.
agent_relevance: Abstraction helps recall of principles for a weaker model and adds little for a strong one using CoT. Run it on a signal (G1), not by default.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Break a problem into easier sub-problems and solve them in order, each using earlier answers. This is decomposition, not relaxation, but it is the usual 'easy version first' prompt.
numbers: SCAN length split with code-davinci-002: least-to-most 99.7% vs chain-of-thought 16.2% (standard prompt 16.7%).
limits: The decomposition prompt was handcrafted for SCAN.
agent_relevance: Easy-first works when the sub-problems follow a fixed template, not when the model must guess them.

source: Frontier LLMs Still Struggle with Simple Reasoning Tasks (2025), Unpuzzles section
finding: Models do worse on trivialised versions of famous puzzles than on the originals, because they recall the original's solution (context corruption). A simplified or relaxed version can pull the model to a wrong memorised answer.
numbers: 97 puzzles with minimal 'unpuzzle' edits. Gap between puzzle and unpuzzle accuracy from 9.1 points (o3) to 54 points (Gemini 1.5). 64-item context-shifted subset tests whether the simple logic is solvable.
limits: One sentence in the text says unpuzzle accuracy was better, probably a typo; the abstract says worse. Direction taken from the abstract.
agent_relevance: A relaxation that resembles a known puzzle can trigger a memorised wrong answer. Restate in neutral terms or change surface names before solving the relaxed version.

source: Hoffmann, Nebel (2001) The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation Through Heuristic Search
finding: FF ignores delete lists, builds a relaxed plan with Graphplan and uses its length as the goal-distance estimate. Helpful actions keep only successors that add a goal needed by the relaxed plan, and enforced hill-climbing searches with it. It was the top fully automatic planner at AIPS-2000.
numbers: Helpful-actions example in Schedule: about 2% of applicable actions kept; 7663 helpful successors out of 523030 across 637 states.
limits: The heuristic is inadmissible and can mislead in dead-end or resource domains.
agent_relevance: The model to copy: relax by deleting negative effects, solve the easy version cheaply, and use its plan both to rank children and to prune them.

source: Hoffmann (2005) Where 'Ignoring Delete Lists' Works: Local Search Topology in Planning Benchmarks (JAIR 24)
finding: Under the ideal relaxed heuristic h+, local-search topology is easy in many benchmark domains. This explains when relaxation works and when it fails.
numbers: 30 domains studied. 24 have no unrecognised dead ends. In 17 of those 24, escape from local minima is bounded by a constant. 12 domains are polynomial for FF's search with h+.
limits: Results are for the idealised h+; FF's approximation matches on dead ends and mostly on topology.
agent_relevance: Relaxation is reliable where sub-goals do not destroy each other. Where actions use up resources the relaxed answer misleads. Test the relaxed score against real results before trusting it.

source: Helmert, Domshlak (2009) Landmarks, Critical Paths and Abstractions: What's the Difference Anyway? (ICAPS)
finding: Proves how four heuristic families relate: delete relaxation, critical paths, abstractions and landmarks. Landmark and additive hmax heuristics do not dominate each other; merge-and-shrink strictly dominates both; pattern databases are incomparable. Introduces the LM-cut heuristic.
numbers: Optimal planning, 22 domains: A* with LM-cut and LM-A* with landmarks each solved more than 400 tasks; next best planner Gamer 312. LM-cut estimates best in all domains except FreeCell and Openstacks.
limits: Dominance results are for admissible heuristics only.
agent_relevance: Different relaxation families give different information. Combining them (portfolio, multi-heuristic) beats picking one.

source: Korf (1997) Finding Optimal Solutions to Rubik's Cube Using Pattern Databases (AAAI-97)
finding: A pattern database stores exact solution lengths for a simplified puzzle (some pieces ignored). It gives an admissible heuristic that made optimal solving of random cubes feasible.
numbers: Corner table 44,089,920 bytes (about 42 MB) at 4 bits per entry. Edge tables 20 MB each; all three 82 MB total. Searches to depth 16 average 9.5 billion nodes in under 4 hours; depth 17 about 122 billion nodes, about two days. Median optimal solution length about 18.
limits: Memory cost; a person chooses the abstraction.
agent_relevance: Abstraction heuristics are computed once and reused. An agent could keep solved easy subproblems in a table.

source: Helmert (2006) The Fast Downward Planning System (JAIR 26)
finding: Describes preferred operators (helpful actions moved into best-first search), deferred evaluation, multi-heuristic best-first search and the causal graph heuristic. Won the classical track of IPC-4 (2004).
numbers: Won the classical track of IPC-4 (2004).
limits: Only the abstract was used for this entry.
agent_relevance: Deferred evaluation and using two heuristics at once are cheap ways to cut cost when scoring candidates is expensive, as with model calls.

source: Hoffmann (2003) The Metric-FF Planning System: Translating Ignoring Delete Lists to Numeric State Variables (JAIR 20)
finding: Extends ignoring delete lists to numeric variables when the task is monotonic, and to linear tasks by preprocessing. Shows a relaxation that needs a validity condition to stay sound.
numbers: Judged one of the two most efficient numeric planners at IPC-3.
limits: Only works for linear tasks after preprocessing.
agent_relevance: A relaxation has a validity condition. State when an operator's relaxed version is safe before using it.

source: Corrêa et al. (2025) end-to-end vs heuristic-generation cost (same paper, Table 2 discussion)
finding: Same model, two uses. Asking the LLM for the plan solved few tasks. Asking it for a heuristic and letting search find the plan solved many more, mostly for non-reasoning models. End-to-end R1 runs took days.
numbers: Gemini 2.0 Flash: 19 solved end-to-end vs 296 with generated heuristics. DeepSeek R1: 174 vs 373. Gemini Thinking: 202 vs 305. DeepSeek V3 end-to-end 48 vs 343 heuristic. Heuristic generation for V3 and R1 cost $0.25 and $6.12 in total.
limits: Heuristic runs use a Python planner with 25 samples and a training-set selection step.
agent_relevance: Strong support for moving the model from 'answer' to 'write the scoring or relaxed solver' slot, with code running the search.
